vignette: Mateo Reyes was thirty-two when the pickup truck on the ridge lost its brakes and careened into his lane during a rain-slicked drive back from a Friday night gig. He remembered the sudden, jarring impact that threw him against the steering wheel, the shattering of glass, and the heavy, metallic smell that filled the cabin before everything went still. When he finally pushed the door open and stumbled onto the wet asphalt, the other driver was already on his phone, unharmed, while Mateo's hands wouldn't stop shaking and his ribs burned with every breath. The accident report was filed, a settlement was offered and quickly signed away by his lawyer, but Mateo never heard the other driver's license plate, and the insurance case closed without explanation. From that night on, quiet moments in his car became impossible. He found himself gripping the wheel at every red light, bracing for a phantom impact, until the only way to steady his pulse was to keep the radio on and stay surrounded by the hum of other people's voices. Over the following months, Mateo's attempts to reconstruct what happened only left him more unsettled. Whenever he sat down to review the police report or speak with his wife, Elena, about the crash, his mind would simply go blank. Fragments surfaced instead: the screech of tires that didn't match the accident, the way his guitar case had flown across the dashboard, the exact angle of the rearview mirror just before the impact. These pieces never lined up, and he felt as though a large portion of the night was simply missing. He avoided pulling at those threads. He had come to believe that keeping his thoughts strictly occupied was the only way to proceed. He stopped driving at night, declined solo booking gigs, and arranged his days around constant activity. He showed up early to studio sessions, lingered after rehearsals, and filled every evening with colleagues and the steady clatter of restaurant crowds. He avoided talking about the accident. He avoided thinking about it. The longer the months stretched, the heavier the certainty settled in Mateo's mind. He was convinced that what had happened to him was deeply unfair, that the lack of consequences for the other driver and the swift closure of his case proved the system would never acknowledge the severity of his ordeal. Alongside that certainty came a sharp, watchful fear of his own temper. He noticed how quickly his frustration could flare when a technician mislabeled a cable or a promoter argued over a payment, and he became certain that if he ever stopped keeping himself distracted, his anger would spiral out of control and drive him to do something terrible. His life felt quietly dismantled by the incident. The constant need to be around people had carved out a new pattern that his bandmates and his wife both noticed. He began canceling soundchecks when the room was too empty, asked producers to keep conversation flowing during breaks, and found himself leaving family dinners early if the talk turned still. Elena had started asking if he was pulling away, but Mateo only tightened his grip on the routine. Now at thirty-five, Mateo walked into the clinic on a Tuesday afternoon with his guitar case resting against his shoulder and a referral slip from his primary care doctor. What finally brought him through the door was the way his hands had begun to tremble during a live set, not from adrenaline, but from a sudden, overwhelming fear that he was losing control of his own mind. He sat on the edge of the intake chair, aware that his therapist was waiting for him to speak, and felt the familiar pull to fill the quiet with a story about a recent gig. He knew he wanted to understand why his own thoughts had become so hostile, and why the memories kept arriving as broken shards instead of a whole story. He was hoping to find a way to sit with the quiet without bracing for impact, and to believe that his life could be rebuilt. He took a slow breath, and prepared to tell them what happened, even if only piece by piece.
